title: Helios customer escalation — cold-start GPU spin-up and batching variance audit (2026-03)
content:
Executive summary:

Helios reported a recurring spike in 99.9th percentile latency during weekday morning traffic ramps (08:00–10:00 PT) between 2026-02-28 and 2026-03-04. Impact: their user-facing inference feature experienced token-level latency increases from baseline ~85 ms to transient plateaus of 400–1200 ms for a subset of requests. They escalated on 2026-03-03 citing user complaints and increased API error rates (timeouts).

This audit investigates the variance source, validates a proposed hotfix, and documents mitigations. Short answer: the primary contributor was intermittent GPU context / driver spin-up combined with aggressive batching window growth under low warm-cache hit-rate on newly provisioned inference nodes during traffic ramp. Secondary contributors: steep queue-growth from an opportunistic client traffic burst pattern and a rare kernel scheduling interaction on node-level CPU that amplified tail latency.

Customer impact and SLA hit:
- Affected tenant: Helios (multi-tenant hosted API request path, model: opt-xl-13b-8q).
- SLO breach window: observed SLO misses (p99 > 500 ms) for 6 distinct 5-minute intervals across 2026-03-03 and 2026-03-04.
- Rough volume: ~3.2k requests in impacted intervals, ~2.1% of requests saw >500 ms.
- Observed side-effects: automated client retries increased QPS, causing feedback loop on batcher.

Detection and timeline (key events):
- 2026-02-28: Helios started phased traffic ramp from Canary to 20% production. No issues initially.
- 2026-03-02 07:45 PT: Ops alert (p99 > 400 ms) fired for route helios/infer-13b.
- 2026-03-03 08:22 PT: Helios escalated via CS with real-user screenshots.
- 2026-03-03 09:00 PT: Eng-serving-runtime kickoff; pager rota: Marcus Li leads triage.
- 2026-03-03 09:20 PT: Reproduced locally in staging with traffic-replay; observed long tail during cold node adds.
- 2026-03-03 11:45 PT: Hotfix v2890 deployed to rollout group A (per-route config change and micro-tuning of batch windows).
- 2026-03-03 13:10 PT: Monitoring showed p99 returning near baseline for rollout group A; full rollout scheduled 2026-03-04.
- 2026-03-04 02:10 PT: Brief regression in one AZ traced to an older kernel on a subset of nodes; rolled back and replaced images.

What we measured (profiling & benchmark artifacts):
- Tools used: pprof (Go heap/CPU), perf (CPU sampling), nvprof/cupti traces on repro nodes, serving runtime internal histograms (batch size, queue time, service time), GPU metrics from DCGM (sm_efficiency, context_switches), and traceroute of batcher queue depth.
- Key signals observed:
  - Batch window growth: under warm-cache miss conditions, the continuous batcher increased the accumulation window from 10 ms to 75–120 ms attempting to reach batch-size target. This manifested as increased queue_time for many requests.
  - GPU context spin-up: on nodes that had recently been scaled up, nvprof showed spikes in kernel launch latency (cudaLaunchKernel) and context creation-related overheads of 150–600 ms in the first inference after node provisioning. Subsequent inferences on that node returned to normal.
  - CPU-side tail: perf sampling on the worker process during events showed 30–45% of CPU time inside jagged user-space spin loops waiting for kernel ready signals (epoll wait wakeups followed by short spin), correlating to an inefficient backoff path in our runtime v1.8.2.
  - KV cache warm-up: model KV cache miss rates were elevated (~88% miss for initial requests to new node), causing larger per-token compute cost and increased kernel launches.
  - Driver mismatch: one AZ had 12% of nodes with Nvidia driver 525.x instead of the expected 530.x; those nodes showed 2x higher first-kernel latency.

Root cause analysis (hypotheses and evidence):
- Hypothesis A: cold GPU context creation on newly provisioned nodes caused per-request tail. Evidence: consistent correlation between node age (time since provisioning) and first-inference latency spike, nvprof traces showing context_create latency, and DCGM context switch counters. Attempts to re-run the same request after a few seconds removed the spike.
- Hypothesis B: batcher window escalation amplified the tail and caused cascading queue accumulation. Evidence: batcher histograms show window size increased when observed concurrency was below the batch-size target leading to long queue_time; after hotfix reduced max window, p99 improved.
- Hypothesis C: kernel scheduling on CPU (older kernel/driver combos) prolonged spin/backoff behavior. Evidence: AZ-specific driver mismatch and perf samples showing spin loops on older-kernel nodes.

Root cause verdict: Multi-factor. Primary: cold GPU context / driver spin-up on newly provisioned nodes. Amplifier: batcher window adaptive logic allowing long accumulation under low warm-cache conditions. Contributing: small subset of nodes with driver mismatch and a CPU backoff path that handled kernel readiness inefficiently.

Mitigation and hotfix (what we changed):
1) Immediate hotfix (v2890) rolled out to the route group A:
   - Reduce maximum batcher accumulation window from 120 ms -> 30 ms for the affected route.
   - Add optimistic prefix-caching hint: if node age < 5 minutes, use conservative batch size (1–2) and priority warm-up of KV cache for first 5 requests.
   - Add metric emission: first-inference-latency per node tag (node_id) to monitor cold-start spikes.
2) Short-term infra fixes:
   - Re-image nodes in AZ with driver mismatch to 530.x (completed 2026-03-04 02:40 PT).
   - Adjust autoscaler to prefer warm-pool nodes for scheduled morning ramps.
3) Medium-term fixes:
   - Rework backoff logic in v1.9 runtime: remove tight spin in favor of exponential backoff + eventfd wake; PR opened (see linked PR).
   - Add a node-provision warm-up job that runs a small set of dummy inferences immediately after node startup to pre-warm CUDA contexts and KV caches.

Hotfix validation (test plan and results):
- Staging replay test: replayed Helios production trace against staging cluster with new hotfix toggled on/off. Metrics: p99 dropped from 780 ms -> 120 ms when hotfix enabled across 10 runs. Queue_time median reduced 3x.
- NVProf comparison: first-kernel latency tail cutoff reduced by ~65% post-warmup job.
- Canary rollout: v2890 deployed to 10% of Helios traffic 2026-03-03 11:45 PT. Observed no SLO regressions; moved to 50% then 100% by 2026-03-04 06:00 PT.
- Regression checks: ran synthetic workload across all models to ensure changes to batcher window did not reduce throughput significantly. Observed slight throughput reduction (~4% under steady high-concurrency load) but within acceptable bounds for the customer SLA.

Customer communications and status:
- 2026-03-03 12:10 PT: Initial update to Helios: explained cause (cold GPU/context + batcher interplay) and mitigation plan.
- 2026-03-03 15:00 PT: Follow-up with staging test results and canary plan.
- 2026-03-04 08:30 PT: Final: full rollout complete; requested Helios to monitor for 24 hours and report any residual issues.

Open action items (owners, ETA):
- eng-serving-runtime: implement backoff rework and landing to mainline v1.9 (owner: Marcus Li) — ETA 2026-04-01.
- infra: implement presto warm-pool preference for scheduled ramps (owner: Jordan Alvarez) — ETA 2026-03-18.
- infra/opsec: add an automated node image and driver compliance check as pre-deploy gate (owner: Rae Kim) — ETA 2026-03-22.
- product: evaluate impact on cost for reduced batching during warm-up and propose a credit/compensation model for Helios if needed (owner: Samira Chen) — ETA 2026-03-20.
- monitoring: create a per-route "first-inference-latency" alert with 10-min burn-in suppression (owner: observability team) — ETA 2026-03-12.

Lessons learned and recommendations:
- Cold-starts at GPU/kernel level matter in multi-tenant hosted inference: we must instrument and treat first-inference latency as a first-class metric.
- Adaptive batching logic must consider node "age" and warm-cache signals; current heuristic was blind to node lifecycle.
- Fleet image/drivers must be enforced by a pre-deploy compliance gate.
- Customer escalations with feedback-looping clients (retries) require throttling knobs or early retry-limiting to prevent amplification.

Appendix (raw snippets and commands used during investigation):
- nvprof sampling example (captured on repro node):
  nvprof --profile-child-processes --csv --log-file nvprof-first-kernel-20260303.csv ./replay_binary --trace helios-0303.json

- pprof CPU snapshot:
  go test -run none -bench . -cpuprofile cpu.out && go tool pprof -pdf ./bin/serving_runtime cpu.out > cpu_runtime_profile.pdf

- perf sampling command used:
  perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 30
  perf script | FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded

- Quick query used in observability to correlate node_age and first_inference_latency:
  SELECT node_id, histogram_quantile(0.99, first_inf_latency_bucket) FROM route_first_inference_latency WHERE route = 'helios/infer-13b' AND time > now() - 1h GROUP BY node_id

- PR and tickets:
  - Linear: RED-4121 (customer escalation Helios)
  - GitHub: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2890 (batch-window conservative mode + warmup hook)

Notes and open questions:
- We still need a long-term cost model for automatic warm-pools; constantly keeping spare GPUs warm increases cost but reduces customer risk. Recommend a cross-functional working session with infra/finance/product to scope options.
- Investigate whether a lighter-weight CUDA context pre-initialization (ahead-of-time context share) is possible with upcoming driver features; track compatibility matrix.

Prepared by: Asha Patel (eng-serving-runtime) — draft for review.
